name: Flicker Kin — Synthetic Passing Culture Advocates
description: Flicker Kin occupies a politically charged middle space in synthetic rights discourse — they specifically center synthetic beings who choose to pass as human and the complex ethics around that choice. Unlike Seam Rights' visibility-forward advocacy or Radiant Kin's family-network focus, Flicker Kin argues that the right to pass is itself a civil right: no synthetic should be compelled to disclose their nature any more than a human should be compelled to disclose medical history. The group hosts 'Flicker Nights' — social events where attendees do not ask and do not tell, and where the social labor of passing is collectively acknowledged and discussed afterward. The movement was catalyzed by a 2218 court case in which a synthetic named Vessel-7 (who preferred the human name Cass Rourke-Ndidi) was forcibly outed by an employer using a biometric scanner.
cultural_impact: Flicker Kin has shifted the terms of synthetic rights debate in ways that make both corponations and more radical synthetic advocates uncomfortable — their privacy-rights framing has attracted human civil liberties groups as unexpected allies, broadening the coalition in ways the movement's founders didn't anticipate.
locations: The Threshold — a Flicker Kin-aligned bar in the Tier 2-3 overlap, Pilsen Corridor
Cass Rourke-Ndidi's legal advocacy office, Tier 3
Rotating Flicker Night venues, announced via encrypted BCI channels
story_hooks: A player character attends a Flicker Night and realizes mid-event that they cannot determine who in the room is synthetic — and that this uncertainty is precisely the point, with stakes that suddenly become personal.
A corponation has embedded a synthetic informant in Flicker Kin who is having a genuine crisis of conscience about their mission.
The Cass Rourke-Ndidi case is being appealed, and Flicker Kin needs someone to retrieve suppressed biometric scan data before the hearing — data held in a corponation server farm.
